name.text: CHEMISTRY_MCQII_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q25 - Actinoids showing oxidation states up to +7

questiontext.text: Which of the following actinoids show oxidation states upto \(+7\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Actinoids exhibit a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids because the \(5f\), \(6d\), and \(7s\) energy levels are very close in energy, allowing all or most valence electrons to participate in bonding.

Step 2: Evaluation
Examine the maximum oxidation states of the given actinoids:
Americium (\(\mathrm{Am}\), \(Z = 95\)) shows oxidation states up to \(+6\).
Plutonium (\(\mathrm{Pu}\), \(Z = 94\)) shows oxidation states from \(+3\) up to \(+7\).
Uranium (\(\mathrm{U}\), \(Z = 92\)) shows oxidation states from \(+3\) up to \(+6\).
Neptunium (\(\mathrm{Np}\), \(Z = 93\)) shows oxidation states from \(+3\) up to \(+7\).

Step 3: Application
Only neptunium (\(\mathrm{Np}\)) and plutonium (\(\mathrm{Pu}\)) attain the \(+7\) oxidation state (for example, in \(\mathrm{NpO}_{5}^{3-}\) and \(\mathrm{PuO}_{5}^{3-}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{Pu}\) and \(\mathrm{Np}\) show oxidation states up to \(+7\).

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MCQII_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q26 - Actinoids with one electron in 6d orbital

questiontext.text: General electronic configuration of actinoids is \((n-2)f^{1-14}(n-1)d^{0-2}ns^2\). Which of the following actinoids have one electron in \(6d\) orbital?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the early actinoids, the \(5f\) and \(6d\) subshells have comparable energies, so one electron frequently occupies the \(6d\) orbital before moving exclusively into \(5f\) for later members.

Step 2: Evaluation
Write the ground-state electronic configurations:
Uranium (\(\mathrm{U}\), \(Z = 92\)): \([\mathrm{Rn}]5f^{3}6d^{1}7s^{2}\) (contains \(1\) electron in \(6d\)).
Neptunium (\(\mathrm{Np}\), \(Z = 93\)): \([\mathrm{Rn}]5f^{4}6d^{1}7s^{2}\) (contains \(1\) electron in \(6d\)).
Plutonium (\(\mathrm{Pu}\), \(Z = 94\)): \([\mathrm{Rn}]5f^{6}6d^{0}7s^{2}\) (\(0\) electrons in \(6d\)).
Americium (\(\mathrm{Am}\), \(Z = 95\)): \([\mathrm{Rn}]5f^{7}6d^{0}7s^{2}\) (\(0\) electrons in \(6d\)).

Step 3: Application
Both \(\mathrm{U}\) and \(\mathrm{Np}\) retain a single electron in the \(6d\) orbital in their ground states, whereas \(\mathrm{Pu}\) and \(\mathrm{Am}\) have empty \(6d\) orbitals.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{U}\) (Atomic no. \(92\)) and \(\mathrm{Np}\) (Atomic no. \(93\)) have one electron in the \(6d\) orbital.

questiontext.text: Which of the following lanthanoids show \(+2\) oxidation state besides the characteristic oxidation state \(+3\) of lanthanoids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While \(+3\) is the characteristic oxidation state for all lanthanoids, certain lanthanoids exhibit \(+2\) or \(+4\) states when doing so yields an extra-stable empty (\(4f^{0}\)), half-filled (\(4f^{7}\)), or completely filled (\(4f^{14}\)) \(4f\) subshell.

Step 2: Evaluation
Check the configurations of the ions:
Cerium (\(\mathrm{Ce}\), \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}\)) shows \(+3\) and \(+4\) (\(4f^{0}\)), not \(+2\).
Europium (\(\mathrm{Eu}\), \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{7}6s^{2}\)) loses its two \(6s\) electrons to form \(\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}\) with a stable half-filled \(4f^{7}\) configuration.
Ytterbium (\(\mathrm{Yb}\), \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{14}6s^{2}\)) loses its two \(6s\) electrons to form \(\mathrm{Yb}^{2+}\) with a stable completely filled \(4f^{14}\) configuration.
Holmium (\(\mathrm{Ho}\)) shows only \(+3\).

Step 3: Application
\(\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Yb}^{2+}\) are well-known divalent lanthanoid ions due to the stability of \(4f^{7}\) and \(4f^{14}\) configurations.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{Eu}\) and \(\mathrm{Yb}\) show the \(+2\) oxidation state besides \(+3\).

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MCQII_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q28 - Ions showing higher spin only magnetic moment

questiontext.text: Which of the following ions show higher spin only magnetic moment value?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The spin-only magnetic moment is given by \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{ B.M.}\), where \(n\) is the number of unpaired electrons. Greater \(n\) yields a higher magnetic moment.

Step 2: Evaluation
Calculate \(n\) and \(\mu\) for each ion:
\(\mathrm{Ti}^{3+}\): \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{1}\), \(n = 1 \implies \mu = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\text{ B.M.}\)
\(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\): \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{5}\), \(n = 5 \implies \mu = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ B.M.}\)
\(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\): \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{6}\), \(n = 4 \implies \mu = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{ B.M.}\)
\(\mathrm{Co}^{3+}\): \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{6}\), \(n = 4 \implies \mu = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{ B.M.}\)

Step 3: Application
Among these ions, \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) has the maximum number of unpaired electrons (\(n = 5\)) and hence the highest spin-only magnetic moment (\(5.92\text{ B.M.}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) shows the higher spin-only magnetic moment value.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MCQII_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q29 - Transition elements forming MF3 type fluorides

questiontext.text: Transition elements form binary compounds with halogens. Which of the following elements will form \(\mathrm{MF}_3\) type compounds?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fluorine, being the most electronegative halogen, stabilises higher oxidation states of transition metals. However, the ability to form a trifluoride \(\mathrm{MF}_{3}\) depends on whether the \(+3\) oxidation state of the metal is stable.

Step 2: Evaluation
Check the stability of the \(+3\) state for each metal with fluorine:
Chromium (\(\mathrm{Cr}\)) readily forms \(\mathrm{CrF}_{3}\) (\(\mathrm{Cr}\) in \(+3\) state).
Cobalt (\(\mathrm{Co}\)) forms \(\mathrm{CoF}_{3}\) (\(\mathrm{Co}\) in \(+3\) state), as fluorine stabilises \(\mathrm{Co(III)}\).
Copper (\(\mathrm{Cu}\)) forms \(\mathrm{CuF}_{2}\) (and not \(\mathrm{CuF}_{3}\) under normal conditions, since \(\mathrm{Cu(III)}\) is unstable).
Nickel (\(\mathrm{Ni}\)) forms \(\mathrm{NiF}_{2}\) (and not \(\mathrm{NiF}_{3}\)).

Step 3: Application
Both chromium and cobalt form stable \(\mathrm{MF}_{3}\)-type fluorides (\(\mathrm{CrF}_{3}\) and \(\mathrm{CoF}_{3}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{Cr}\) and \(\mathrm{Co}\) form \(\mathrm{MF}_{3}\) type compounds.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MCQII_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q30 - Species that do not act as oxidising agents

questiontext.text: Which of the following will not act as oxidising agents?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Group 6 of the transition series, the stability of the \(+6\) oxidation state increases down the group (\(\mathrm{Cr(VI)} < \mathrm{Mo(VI)} < \mathrm{W(VI)}\)). A species in a high oxidation state acts as a strong oxidising agent only if it can be readily reduced to a lower oxidation state.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{CrO}_{3}\) and \(\mathrm{CrO}_{4}^{2-}\) contain \(\mathrm{Cr(VI)}\), which is less stable than \(\mathrm{Cr(III)}\) in acidic medium and therefore acts as a strong oxidising agent.
In contrast, \(\mathrm{MoO}_{3}\) and \(\mathrm{WO}_{3}\) contain \(\mathrm{Mo(VI)}\) and \(\mathrm{W(VI)}\), which are very stable and resist reduction.

Step 3: Application
Because \(\mathrm{Mo(VI)}\) and \(\mathrm{W(VI)}\) are highly stable, \(\mathrm{MoO}_{3}\) and \(\mathrm{WO}_{3}\) do not act as oxidising agents.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{MoO}_{3}\) and \(\mathrm{WO}_{3}\) will not act as oxidising agents.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MCQII_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q31 - Reason for +4 oxidation state of cerium

questiontext.text: Although \(+3\) is the characteristic oxidation state for lanthanoids but cerium also shows \(+4\) oxidation state because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cerium (\(\mathrm{Ce}\), \(Z = 58\)) has the ground-state electronic configuration \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
When cerium loses all four valence electrons (\(4f^{1}\), \(5d^{1}\), and \(6s^{2}\)) to form \(\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}\), its electronic configuration becomes \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{0}\). This corresponds both to an empty \(f\)-subshell (\(f^{0}\) configuration) and to the stable noble gas configuration of xenon.

Step 3: Application
The stability gained by attaining a noble gas configuration and an \(f^{0}\) configuration favours the formation of \(\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}\) despite its high fourth ionisation enthalpy.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, cerium shows the \(+4\) oxidation state because it has a tendency to attain noble gas configuration and \(f^{0}\) configuration.

answer.text: it has a tendency to attain noble gas configuration
it has a tendency to attain \(f^0\) configuration

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MATCHING_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MT_Q52 - Catalysts and their industrial or organic processes

questiontext.text: Match the catalysts given in Column I with the processes given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transition metals and their compounds serve as specific catalysts in industrial and organic reactions due to their variable oxidation states and ability to adsorb reactants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Match each catalyst to its corresponding process:
\(\mathrm{Ni}\) in the presence of hydrogen catalyses the hydrogenation of unsaturated vegetable oils to solid ghee.
\(\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\) is used in the Sandmeyer reaction to convert benzene diazonium chloride into chlorobenzene.
\(\mathrm{V}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}\) catalyses the oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\) to \(\mathrm{SO}_{3}\) in the Contact process for manufacturing sulphuric acid.
Finely divided iron catalyses the synthesis of ammonia from \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) in Haber's process.
\(\mathrm{TiCl}_{4} + \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{CH}_{3})_{3}\) is the Ziegler–Natta catalyst used in polymerisation of alkenes.

Step 3: Application
The remaining item, decomposition of \(\mathrm{KClO}_{3}\), is catalysed by \(\mathrm{MnO}_{2}\) (not listed in Column I).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matches are: \(\mathrm{Ni}\) with hydrogen \(\rightarrow\) Vegetable oil to ghee; \(\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\) \(\rightarrow\) Sandmeyer reaction; \(\mathrm{V}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{5}\) \(\rightarrow\) Contact process; Finely divided iron \(\rightarrow\) Haber's Process; \(\mathrm{TiCl}_{4} + \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{CH}_{3})_{3}\) \(\rightarrow\) Zieglar Natta catalyst.

questiontext.text: Match the compounds/elements given in Column I with uses given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lanthanoids and their oxides/alloys have specialised industrial applications in metallurgy, catalysis, phosphors, and pyrophoric alloys.

Step 2: Evaluation
Match each item:
Lanthanoid oxides are used as phosphors in television screens.
Lanthanoid is used in the production of iron alloy (alloy steels for plates and pipes).
Misch metal is an alloy of lanthanoid metal (~95%) and iron (~5%) with traces of \(\mathrm{S}\), \(\mathrm{C}\), \(\mathrm{Ca}\), and \(\mathrm{Al}\).
A magnesium-based alloy containing misch metal is a constituent of bullets, shells, and lighter flints.
Mixed oxides of lanthanoids are employed as catalysts in petroleum cracking.

Step 3: Application
Each entry in Column I pairs uniquely with its corresponding industrial use or composition in Column II.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matches are: Lanthanoid oxide \(\rightarrow\) Television screen; Lanthanoid \(\rightarrow\) Production of iron alloy; Misch metal \(\rightarrow\) Lanthanoid metal + iron; Magnesium based alloy is constituent of \(\rightarrow\) Bullets; Mixed oxides of lanthanoids are employed \(\rightarrow\) Petroleum cracking.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MATCHING_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MT_Q54 - Transition metal properties and corresponding metals

questiontext.text: Match the properties given in Column I with the metals given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transition metals display characteristic maximum oxidation states and high melting points depending on their valence \(d\)- and \(s\)-electron counts.

Step 2: Evaluation
Match each property:
Osmium (\(\mathrm{Os}\), Group 8, \(5d\)-series) can show the \(+8\) oxidation state (as in \(\mathrm{OsO}_{4}\)).
Manganese (\(\mathrm{Mn}\), Group 7, \(3d\)-series) can show up to the \(+7\) oxidation state (as in \(\mathrm{Mn}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}\) and \(\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}\)).
Chromium (\(\mathrm{Cr}\)) has the highest melting point (\(2180\text{ K}\)) among the \(3d\) transition elements.

Step 3: Application
Iron (\(\mathrm{Fe}\)) serves as the unmatched distractor in Column II.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matches are: An element which can show +8 oxidation state \(\rightarrow\) Os; 3d block element that can show upto +7 oxidation state \(\rightarrow\) Mn; 3d block element with highest melting point \(\rightarrow\) Cr.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MATCHING_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MT_Q55 - Oxidation states of manganese and lanthanoids

questiontext.text: Match the statements given in Column I with the oxidation states given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Manganese exhibits oxidation states from \(+2\) to \(+7\), while lanthanoids exhibit \(+3\) as their characteristic oxidation state.

Step 2: Evaluation
Match each statement:
In \(\mathrm{MnO}_{2}\), let the oxidation state of \(\mathrm{Mn}\) be \(x\): \(x + 2(-2) = 0 \implies x = +4\).
The most stable oxidation state of \(\mathrm{Mn}\) in aqueous solution is \(+2\) (\(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) has a half-filled \(3d^{5}\) configuration).
In oxides, oxygen forms multiple bonds with manganese, stabilising its highest oxidation state of \(+7\) (as in \(\mathrm{Mn}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}\)).
The characteristic oxidation state common to all lanthanoids is \(+3\).

Step 3: Application
\(+5\) is the unused distractor in Column II.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matches are: Oxidation state of Mn in \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\) is \(\rightarrow\) +4; Most stable oxidation state of Mn is \(\rightarrow\) +2; Most stable oxidation state of Mn in oxides is \(\rightarrow\) +7; Characteristic oxidation state of lanthanoids is \(\rightarrow\) +3.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MATCHING_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MT_Q56 - Aqueous transition metal salt solutions and their colours

questiontext.text: Match the solutions given in Column I and the colours given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrated transition metal ions exhibit characteristic colours in aqueous solution due to \(d\text{-}d\) electronic transitions, while \(d^{10}\) ions are colourless.

Step 2: Evaluation
Match each salt with the colour of its aqueous solution:
\(\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}\cdot 7\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\), \(3d^{6}\)) gives a pale green solution.
\(\mathrm{NiCl}_{2}\cdot 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) (\(\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\), \(3d^{8}\)) gives a green solution.
\(\mathrm{MnCl}_{2}\cdot 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) (\(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\), \(3d^{5}\)) gives a light pink solution.
\(\mathrm{CoCl}_{2}\cdot 6\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) (\(\mathrm{Co}^{2+}\), \(3d^{7}\)) gives a pink solution.
\(\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\) (\(\mathrm{Cu}^{+}\), \(3d^{10}\)) has no unpaired \(d\)-electrons and is colourless.

Step 3: Application
Blue is the distractor in Column II (characteristic of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\), which is not listed in Column I).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matches are: \(\mathrm{FeSO}_4\cdot 7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) \(\rightarrow\) Pale green; \(\mathrm{NiCl}_2\cdot 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) \(\rightarrow\) Green; \(\mathrm{MnCl}_2\cdot 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) \(\rightarrow\) Light pink; \(\mathrm{CoCl}_2\cdot 6\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) \(\rightarrow\) Pink; \(\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\) \(\rightarrow\) Colourless.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_MATCHING_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_MT_Q58 - Ionisation enthalpies, carbonyls, and atomisation enthalpy of 3d metals

questiontext.text: Match the properties given in Column I with the metals given in Column II.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionisation enthalpies, metal carbonyl formation, and enthalpies of atomisation of \(3d\) metals depend on their \(d\)-electron configurations and metallic bonding strengths.

Step 2: Evaluation
Match each property:
Copper (\(\mathrm{Cu}\)) has the highest second ionisation enthalpy among \(3d\) metals because removing a second electron disrupts the stable completely filled \(3d^{10}\) configuration of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{+}\).
Zinc (\(\mathrm{Zn}\)) has the highest third ionisation enthalpy because removing a third electron disrupts the completely filled \(3d^{10}\) configuration of \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\).
In the hexacarbonyl \(\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{CO})_{6}\), the metal \(\mathrm{M}\) is \(\mathrm{Cr}\) (forming \(\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{CO})_{6}\), following the 18-electron rule).
Among the listed metals (\(\mathrm{Co}, \mathrm{Cr}, \mathrm{Cu}, \mathrm{Zn}, \mathrm{Ni}\)), nickel (\(\mathrm{Ni}\)) has the highest enthalpy of atomisation (\(430\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Application
Cobalt (\(\mathrm{Co}\)) is the unmatched distractor in Column II.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matches are: Element with highest second ionisation enthalpy \(\rightarrow\) Cu; Element with highest third ionisation enthalpy \(\rightarrow\) Zn; M in \(\mathrm{M(CO)}_6\) is \(\rightarrow\) Cr; Element with highest heat of atomisation \(\rightarrow\) Ni.

questiontext.text:
In the following question a statement of assertion followed by a statement of reason is given. Choose the correct answer out of the following choices.

Assertion : \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) iodide is not known.
Reason : \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) oxidises \(\mathrm{I}^{-}\) to iodine.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The stability of a transition metal halide depends on the redox potentials of the metal cation and the halide anion.

Step 2: Evaluation
The assertion is true: copper(II) iodide (\(\mathrm{CuI}_{2}\)) does not exist under normal conditions. The reason is also true: \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) is a sufficiently strong oxidising agent to oxidise \(\mathrm{I}^{-}\) to \(\mathrm{I}_{2}\), while reducing itself to \(\mathrm{Cu}^{+}\) to form insoluble \(\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{I}_{2}\):
\(2\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{I}_{2}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{I}_{2}\)

Step 3: Application
Because this spontaneous redox reaction converts any \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{I}^{-}\) mixture into \(\mathrm{Cu}_{2}\mathrm{I}_{2}\) and \(\mathrm{I}_{2}\), the reason directly explains why \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) iodide is not known.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both assertion and reason are true, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.
Assertion is not true but reason is true.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_ASSERTIONREASON_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q60 - Difficulty in separating Zr and Hf

questiontext.text:
In the following question a statement of assertion followed by a statement of reason is given. Choose the correct answer out of the following choices.

Assertion : Separation of \(\mathrm{Zr}\) and \(\mathrm{Hf}\) is difficult.
Reason : Because \(\mathrm{Zr}\) and \(\mathrm{Hf}\) lie in the same group of the periodic table.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elements in the same group normally show a noticeable increase in atomic size down the group, making their chemical separation feasible. However, lanthanoid contraction alters this trend between the \(4d\) and \(5d\) series.

Step 2: Evaluation
The assertion is true: separating \(\mathrm{Zr}\) and \(\mathrm{Hf}\) is extremely difficult. The reason is also true: both \(\mathrm{Zr}\) and \(\mathrm{Hf}\) belong to Group 4 of the periodic table.

Step 3: Application
However, merely lying in the same group does not make separation difficult (for instance, \(\mathrm{Ti}\) is also in Group 4 and is easily separated from \(\mathrm{Zr}\)). The real reason for the difficulty in separating \(\mathrm{Zr}\) and \(\mathrm{Hf}\) is lanthanoid contraction, which gives them nearly identical atomic and ionic radii and hence almost identical chemical properties.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both assertion and reason are true, but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.

answer.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.
Assertion is not true but reason is true.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_ASSERTIONREASON_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q61 - Complex formation tendency of actinoids vs lanthanoids

questiontext.text:
In the following question a statement of assertion followed by a statement of reason is given. Choose the correct answer out of the following choices.

Assertion : Actinoids form relatively less stable complexes as compared to lanthanoids.
Reason : Actinoids can utilise their \(5f\) orbitals along with \(6d\) orbitals in bonding but lanthanoids do not use their \(4f\) orbital for bonding.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Complex formation ability in \(f\)-block elements depends on the nuclear charge, ionic size, and the availability of valence orbitals for covalent bonding.

Step 2: Evaluation
The assertion is false: actinoids actually have a much greater tendency to form complexes and form more stable complexes than lanthanoids, due to higher nuclear charge, smaller size for a given oxidation state, and availability of \(5f\) orbitals.
The reason is true: actinoid \(5f\) orbitals are less deeply buried than lanthanoid \(4f\) orbitals, allowing actinoids to use both \(5f\) and \(6d\) orbitals in bonding, whereas lanthanoids do not use their deeply buried \(4f\) orbitals for bonding.

Step 3: Application
Since the assertion is false and the reason is true, the statement pair matches the case where the assertion is not true but the reason is true.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Assertion is not true, but reason is true.

answer.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.
Assertion is not true but reason is true.

name.text: CHEMISTRY_ASSERTIONREASON_DANDFBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q62 - Inability of copper to liberate hydrogen from acids

questiontext.text:
In the following question a statement of assertion followed by a statement of reason is given. Choose the correct answer out of the following choices.

Assertion : \(\mathrm{Cu}\) cannot liberate hydrogen from acids.
Reason : Because it has positive electrode potential.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A metal displaces \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) gas from non-oxidising acids only if its standard reduction potential \(E^\circ_{\mathrm{M}^{n+}/\mathrm{M}}\) is negative (less than \(0.00\text{ V}\) for \(\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H}_{2}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
The assertion is true: copper does not liberate hydrogen gas from dilute acids.
The reason is also true: copper has a positive standard electrode potential (\(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\)).

Step 3: Application
Because \(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} > E^\circ_{\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H}_{2}}\), copper is a weaker reducing agent than \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) and cannot reduce \(\mathrm{H}^{+}\) ions to \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\). Thus, the reason correctly explains the assertion.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both assertion and reason are true, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

answer.text: Both assertion and reason are true, and reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
Both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.
Assertion is not true but reason is true.

questiontext.text:
In the following question a statement of assertion followed by a statement of reason is given. Choose the correct answer out of the following choices.

Assertion : The highest oxidation state of osmium is \(+8\).
Reason : Osmium is a \(5d\)-block element.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Osmium (\(\mathrm{Os}\), \(Z = 76\)) belongs to Group 8 and the \(5d\) transition series, with valence electronic configuration \(5d^{6}6s^{2}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The assertion is true: osmium exhibits a maximum oxidation state of \(+8\) (for example, in \(\mathrm{OsO}_{4}\)).
The reason is also true: osmium is a \(5d\)-block element.

Step 3: Application
However, being a \(5d\)-block element does not by itself explain the \(+8\) oxidation state (other \(5d\) elements do not show \(+8\)). Osmium shows \(+8\) because it has \(8\) valence electrons (\(5d^{6}6s^{2}\)) and can share all of them in covalent/multiple bonds with highly electronegative oxygen atoms.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both assertion and reason are true, but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.
